lxc_324fd01b279538da.text: This lesson teaches six strange traditions from six places.

lxc_d56531f4fdf0c298.text: Each part explains what people do, where they do it, why they do it, and how the day or ceremony works.

lxc_28ac9a68b5e017d0.text: La Tomatina is a tomato fight in the town of Buñol, in Spain.

lxc_97eb42845e8fcf2b.text: It is a street festival, not a meal.

lxc_a8c622e6a22898c2.text: The town's own account starts on the last Wednesday of August in 1945.

lxc_eafafda155515f64.text: Young people were in the Plaza del Pueblo to watch a parade of giants and big heads.

lxc_b73e93b88df67e3e.text: A participant fell and hit a vegetable stall.

lxc_ac23ea8d08082024.text: The crowd threw tomatoes until the police stopped the fight.

lxc_e7d649c206311fe2.text: The next year, people brought tomatoes from home and did it again.

lxc_cabdc82d36a0cd9e.text: In the early 1950s the police banned it, because they did not want it to become a tradition.

lxc_32054b868d3086f0.text: The town asked for the festival back.

lxc_c232b3a11f37ae38.text: It was allowed again and became an official local festival.

lxc_f83bb9b1ddf56945.text: In 2002 Spain named La Tomatina a Fiesta of International Tourist Interest.

lxc_e4d6fea53a66d11f.text: The town now runs the day on a clear clock.

lxc_b8d459ea0caef3aa.text: On the 2025 municipal timetable, the Palo Jabón, a slippery pole, started at 11:00.

lxc_371362d8f20d2988.text: The tomato festival itself ran from 12:00 to 13:00.

lxc_1d57dda63b86eb5d.text: At 13:00, cleaning of the route and the nearby streets began.

lxc_5b8e29c47b7224ad.text: So the famous part is one organized hour in the middle of the day, not an all-day food fight.

lxc_cf39b78829cee86a.text: Up Helly Aa is the big fire festival in Lerwick, the main town of Shetland, in Scotland.

lxc_78510610e5d0d7f1.text: It remembers Shetland's Norse past, but the organized festival people see today grew in Lerwick in the late 1800s.

lxc_28e1c84b872c543b.text: Around 1870, local men gave it the name Up Helly Aa, moved it toward the end of January, and added costumes and torches.

lxc_1c649ad899366ff6.text: A Viking longship, called the galley, joined in the late 1880s.

lxc_53aa558244c8b40f.text: The leader's title, Guizer Jarl, dates from 1906.

lxc_334ede0af0953d3e.text: The festival is on the last Tuesday of January.

lxc_7794f3776cca5bd5.text: Volunteers build the galley from late October.

lxc_909bc099fd816ee1.text: The Guizer Jarl chooses its colour, and that colour stays secret until the day.

lxc_dad23d578649c0d9.text: The Guizer Jarl is the chief guizer, the leader of the Jarl Squad.

lxc_a50cad9836ea737d.text: The other squads, about forty-five of them, wear fancy-dress suits.

lxc_343baee4b14f589f.text: Almost a thousand people carry torches.

lxc_1c8f3b5aa69472f1.text: The Jarl Squad marches from the early morning.

lxc_d07f4c91d2c1a187.text: At the Town Hall, the Guizer Jarl receives the freedom of the town for twenty-four hours.

lxc_bc6a9d1bce80b3a5.text: At 19:30 a signal lights more than nine hundred torches.

lxc_dac3cb17f7ba8d86.text: The Jarl stands at the helm of the galley.

lxc_859e45b21723a6e9.text: The procession ends at the burning site on the King George V playing field, and the public stays outside that site.

lxc_72b9348e55f0425d.text: Then the squads visit eleven halls.

lxc_f9528b5bf850351c.text: In each hall they perform a short act and dance with the guests.

lxc_987dcea4d5365b30.text: They often finish near breakfast on Wednesday, and that Wednesday is a public holiday in Shetland.

lxc_d17e77879a689e69.text: In Bulgaria, masked dancers are widely known as kukeri.

lxc_33c134eeb3ac66a3.text: A workshop at the National Museum of History in Sofia teaches that Kukeri dances drive away evil, and that the costumes are both scary and beautiful.

lxc_70e6c5414dab1c68.text: The concrete winter feast on the UNESCO list is in the Pernik region.

lxc_60d997378ba7ae9c.text: There the feast is called Surova, and the masked groups are called Survakari.

lxc_971e8828d997d6f5.text: Surova is on 13 and 14 January, the New Year on the old calendar.

lxc_c9f4f6c4fac16f2c.text: On the first night, men, women, and children put on masks and costumes.

lxc_34d3378f0f745bfa.text: They go to the village centre, light fires, and play with the crowd.

lxc_4ad362b18149b1e7.text: Some people take special roles: the leader, the newly-weds, the priest, and the bear.

lxc_dfe12b98703efb7e.text: Early the next morning they walk through the village and visit houses.

lxc_01adcf43f9df9da3.text: The bear pretends to grab people, and that action is for good health.

lxc_a72e97288309fba7.text: Hosts wait with a meal and gifts.

lxc_33ea4af6db0b337d.text: Later the Survakari share those gifts, often with orphans and poor people.

lxc_af8cd3b4b813d7c8.text: Families collect materials all year, and adults teach children how to make the masks.

lxc_096dfb93f755469f.text: Land diving is a ritual on Pentecost Island, in Vanuatu.

lxc_1cc48ed2e9a4d6e6.text: Men jump from a tall wooden tower made of logs and vines.

lxc_1477835e067099c2.text: The Vanuatu Tourism Office says the tower can reach about 30 metres.

lxc_5cdf0ff515c90051.text: The divers are held by vines, not ropes.

lxc_10e83d50c7a95cb1.text: The vines are chosen for strength and flexibility, and each jumper calculates the length so he can land safely.

lxc_0c783d62778d8b4b.text: People do this to help bring a good yam harvest.

lxc_abba9eab472ed1b4.text: Yams are an important food crop.

lxc_c0efe03a3126bc3c.text: In some communities the dive is also a step toward adult life.

lxc_f7e6598835caa1a9.text: In 2026 the public dives run on Saturdays from April through June, in the yam season.

lxc_dc13ee4e7e935ca8.text: On Pentecost Island the meaning is the harvest, courage, and the community, not a sport show.

lxc_19b75a5af15565a2.text: Famadihana is a family ceremony in Madagascar.

lxc_f0609b61118c2a27.text: People also call it the turning of the bones.

lxc_f2ac661ca12931bf.text: Among the Merina and the Betsileo, in the highlands, it is a celebration of family and of life together.

lxc_56c2024e4289195b.text: It is not a horror show.

lxc_b8622438a3b2d899.text: Two to three years after a burial, the family takes the ancestor from the tomb.

lxc_b8177642f416be29.text: They wrap the ancestor in a new silk lamba, a cloth made for this moment.

lxc_a1c22533e7382e4f.text: The family and the community greet the ancestor and dance.

lxc_e34de3c2f8b16fba.text: Then they return the ancestor to the family tomb.

lxc_4315d7425d476c98.text: The museum that records this ceremony calls it a joyful occasion, not a time of grief.

lxc_d47772cc6fb65fe6.text: Fresh cloth, dancing, and coming home to the tomb are signs of continued care.

lxc_d39bbd4ca71938c1.text: On 31 December, young men dressed as Namahage visit houses on the Oga Peninsula, in Akita, Japan.

lxc_4e513f289914fabc.text: They wear masks and straw coats, with straw guards on their legs and straw boots for the snow.

lxc_1bedc995062a0136.text: For people in Oga, these visitors are gods who come with the New Year.

lxc_1d7e9fd22dc21f30.text: They also bring protection from illness and disaster, hope for a good harvest, and food from the mountains and the sea.

lxc_8da46cfa18d4a369.text: At the door they shout questions about crybabies, children who do not listen to their parents, and whether the woman of the house wakes up early.

lxc_76fd230f2c2ac201.text: The hosts welcome them with traditional food and sake.

lxc_74046c686089b040.text: Some Namahage carry a large kitchen knife.

lxc_2dd0c58594795480.text: It is a symbol, not a weapon for harm.

lxc_21e8d702b92fe943.text: People who sit too long by the fire get blisters, called namomi.

lxc_6be24592e39dd75b.text: "Peeling the blisters" is a picture of leaving laziness behind, and that idea became the name Namahage.

lxc_ca81f7f788c06dfd.text: People in Oga tell more than one old story about where the Namahage come from, so this lesson stays with the meaning of the visit.

lxc_68818f8dc5d1856e.text: The visits used to follow the lunar New Year.

lxc_705f1e3107686077.text: In 1978, Oga's Namahage became an Important Intangible Cultural Asset.

lxc_91f87fa101c3b8cd.text: In 2018, UNESCO inscribed Raiho-shin, ritual visits of deities in masks and costumes.

lxc_b6c408db800b284d.text: Oga City says Oga no Namahage is one of the ten rituals in that inscription.

lxc_b532fda3efde9105.text: In a Raiho-shin visit, local people in frightening masks scold laziness, teach children, and receive a meal.

lxc_14baf8a5f62567a4.text: The scary face is part of a community welcome.
